title: Weather sensitivity by zone and weather-adjusted load: was it the cold, or demand?
concepts: OLS: load on HDD and CDD
coefficients in MW per degree day
Durbin-Watson: are the intervals too narrow?

explain.prompt: Answer the trader's question — “North load was up this January: more demand, or just colder?” — in 5–7 sentences. Use the coefficients (with their units and intervals), the January–February comparison of actual and weather-adjusted load, and say clearly what a weather-adjusted load is and is not.
rubric: Coefficients read as MW of average daily load per degree day: NORTH +261 MW per HDD [259, 263], CENTRAL +174 [170, 178], SOUTH +60 [58, 63]; cooling: SOUTH +321 MW per CDD [312, 330], CENTRAL +112 [54, 170]. Signs are as expected (more heating or cooling degree days, more load) and the weekend dummy is NORTH −1,067, CENTRAL −1,665, SOUTH −822 MW. The intervals are too narrow: Durbin-Watson is 0.61–0.78, the daily errors are autocorrelated.

NORTH's cooling coefficient (+130 MW per CDD) rests on 4 warm days: its interval [−142, +401] says the data cannot measure it — a coefficient with no support should not be used, whatever its point value.

January–February 2024 was much colder than 2023 (NORTH HDD 18.8 vs 15.5 per day). Actual NORTH load rose 5.4 % (12,689 → 13,379 MW); weather-adjusted load fell 1.4 % (12,879 → 12,697). CENTRAL: +0.9 % actual, −3.7 % adjusted; SOUTH: +1.1 % actual, −2.8 % adjusted.
So the January increase is a weather effect; underlying demand was lower in every zone. The trader's 'growth' is the cold.

Weather-adjusted load = actual load − estimated effect of the actual weather relative to normal weather (the zone's 30-year mean HDD/CDD for that calendar month). It is a model-based counterfactual, not an observed load and not a forecast.

Limits: the adjustment is only as good as the regression (linear degree days, one station per zone, a constant level over two years); what remains after adjustment mixes genuine demand change, holidays, prices and noise — the adjustment does not explain every change in demand.
